entities.name: Warner Bros. Entertainment
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Warner Bros. Entertainment, founded in 1923 by the four Warner brothers (Harry, Albert, Sam, Jack) and now part of Warner Bros. Discovery, is the studio that introduced synchronized sound to cinema (The Jazz Singer, 1927), created the gangster film genre (Little Caesar, The Public Enemy, 1931), and produced the highest-grossing film franchise in history (the DC Extended Universe, Harry Potter franchise at $9.7 billion, and Looney Tunes), making it one of the most consequential creative institutions of the 20th century. The 1927 Jazz Singer — featuring Al Jolson speaking (not just singing) — ended the silent film era overnight.

The Jazz Singer (1927) was not the first sound film but the first commercially successful one — Warner Bros. had bet the company on the Vitaphone synchronized-sound system, nearly bankrupting itself. The gamble succeeded beyond imagination: silent cinema ended within two years. Warner's 1930s gangster cycle (James Cagney, Edward G. Robinson, Humphrey Bogart) defined American cinema's most influential genre. Casablanca (1942) is consistently voted one of the greatest films ever made; Citizen Kane was distributed (not produced) by RKO but Warner produced comparable landmark films.

Warner's DC Comics ownership (Superman 1978, Batman 1989, Dark Knight trilogy, Aquaman, Wonder Woman) and Harry Potter ($9.7 billion franchise from J.K. Rowling's books) plus Looney Tunes (Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck) give it three of entertainment's most commercially durable franchises. The AT&T acquisition (2018, $85 billion) and subsequent Discovery merger (2022) transformed Warner into Warner Bros. Discovery, with the HBO Max (now Max) streaming service competing with Netflix.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Warner Bros.' introduction of synchronized sound in The Jazz Singer (1927) — which ended silent cinema overnight — is the single most disruptive technological event in film history, and the studio's subsequent 100-year run from gangster films to Harry Potter makes it American cinema's most historically consequential studio.
